stories.headline: IAF's record IL-76 landing at Nyoma; Rajnath calls for highest readiness
stories.summary: An Indian Air Force IL-76MD transport aircraft landed at the Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh at an altitude of 13,629 feet, described as a world record for the highest-altitude landing by an aircraft of its class. The airbase lies roughly 25 km from the China border and is being projected as a boost to India's strategic airlift and logistics reach along the Line of Actual Control. On the same day, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, addressing personnel at a key airbase near the China frontier, warned of evolving threats and asked the armed forces to maintain the highest levels of operational readiness, cautioning that adversaries seek to exploit vulnerabilities. He reviewed the Army's LAC infrastructure and operational preparedness and appreciated initiatives aimed at strengthening ties with local communities. In his remarks on the changing character of warfare, he flagged social media rumour-mongering, drone use and cyberattacks as instruments now routinely deployed by adversaries.
stories.whyItMatters: High-altitude airlift capability and LAC infrastructure are core to India's deterrence posture and border-management strategy, while the emphasis on drones, cyber and information warfare maps directly onto the GS-III internal security syllabus.

perspectives.take: Frames the visit around the Defence Minister's warning on evolving threats and 'vulnerabilities', and his review of Army infrastructure and community outreach along the LAC — a sober, official-account framing.

static.topic: India-China border infrastructure and high-altitude airlift capability
static.syllabusNode: Security — Border Management and Internal Security
static.whatIsIt: India has been upgrading roads, advanced landing grounds (ALGs), helipads and storage along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) to shorten reaction times and sustain troops in the high Himalaya. Nyoma, in the Changthang region of eastern Ladakh, is one such airfield whose usability by large transport aircraft like the IL-76MD extends the reach of strategic airlift to the frontier.
static.background: India-China border management rests on the LAC, patrolled by the ITBP and the Army, with periodic confidence-building mechanisms such as the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) and the Special Representatives talks on the boundary question. Infrastructure gaps on the Indian side were highlighted after the 2020 Galwan clash, prompting accelerated road, tunnel and airfield works in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh. The Darbuk–Shyok–Daulat Beg Oldi road and the Sela and Shinkun La tunnels are part of this build-out.
static.geography: Nyoma lies in the cold desert of the Changthang plateau in eastern Ladakh, at about 13,629 feet and roughly 25 km from the China border; the sector faces extreme cold, low oxygen and a short construction season.
static.socioEconomic: The area is home to the Changpa pastoralist community; civil-military cooperation and border-village development schemes such as the Vibrant Villages Programme are intended to check out-migration and sustain local livelihoods.
static.whyInNews: An IAF IL-76MD landed at Nyoma at 13,629 feet — reported as the highest-altitude landing by an aircraft of its class — coinciding with the Defence Minister's review of LAC infrastructure and readiness.
static.wayForward: Sustained investment in all-weather connectivity, airfield hardening, drone-based logistics and habitat technology, balanced with environmental safeguards and local community welfare, would convert infrastructure into durable deterrence.
prelimsPointers: The India-China border is about 3,488 km long and is guarded by the ITBP along with the Army.
Nyoma is an advanced landing ground in eastern Ladakh's Changthang region, close to the LAC.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how border infrastructure and airlift capability shape India's deterrence and crisis-response options along the LAC.

static.topic: Hybrid and non-kinetic warfare: drones, cyberattacks and information operations
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security: Cyber and Emerging Threats
static.whatIsIt: Modern conflict increasingly blends conventional military action with non-kinetic tools — unmanned systems, cyber intrusions, disinformation and social-media manipulation — aimed at eroding public confidence and degrading critical systems without open hostilities.
static.background: India's internal security architecture is coordinated by the Ministry of Home Affairs with agencies such as the Intelligence Bureau, the NIA (2008) and CERT-In, the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response. The SAMADHAN doctrine guides counter-left-wing-extremism strategy, while NATGRID and Integrated Command and Control Centres support intelligence-led policing. Drone threats have prompted counter-UAS protocols for critical installations and border areas.
static.socioEconomic: Widespread smartphone and social-media penetration makes disinformation campaigns cheap and fast, with consequences for communal harmony, electoral integrity and public trust in institutions.
static.whyInNews: The Defence Minister stated that adversaries spread rumours on social media, deploy drones and launch cyberattacks, describing these as the changing face of warfare.
static.wayForward: Strengthen CERT-In capacity and critical-infrastructure protection, build counter-drone capability, institutionalise media literacy and rapid fact-verification, and integrate cyber and information domains into military doctrine and training.
prelimsPointers: CERT-In is the national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents in India.
The NIA, established in 2008, investigates offences under the NIA Act.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the rise of drones, cyberattacks and disinformation reshapes India's internal security priorities and institutional responses.

static.topic: India's China policy and strategic autonomy

static.whatIsIt: India's approach to China combines firmness on the border with continued diplomatic and economic engagement, pursued within a broader framework of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment across the Quad, BRICS, SCO and the G20.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954), India's foreign policy was reshaped by the 1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad gained salience after 2017. Border tensions since 2020 have tested the balance between deterrence, de-escalation mechanisms and economic ties.
static.whyInNews: The Defence Minister's readiness message and the record IL-76 landing at Nyoma come amid continuing military standoff management and infrastructure competition along the LAC.
static.wayForward: Maintain a credible deterrent posture alongside functioning military and diplomatic channels, diversify supply chains and technology partnerships, and keep border management insulated from wider bilateral engagement.
prelimsPointers: India and Pakistan joined the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2017.
India hosted the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.

stories.headline: Delhi tops global pollution charts as GRAP Stage 3 curbs stay in force
stories.summary: Delhi has been ranked the world's most polluted major city on the eve of Diwali by a Swiss air-quality tracking group, with the city's AQI hovering around 364 — firmly in the 'very poor' band. Restrictions under Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan remain in force even though the index has eased from the 'severe' threshold, since the curbs are lifted only after a sustained improvement in air quality. Enforcement has widened beyond construction sites and vehicles: the Gurgaon district administration has issued notices to at least two law firms for alleged violations of pollution-related office norms. Commentary in the environmental press argues that the annual crisis reflects deeper structural failures rather than a shortage of emergency rules, while the immediate trigger remains the winter combination of low wind, temperature inversion, vehicular and industrial emissions and post-harvest stubble burning in the surrounding states.
stories.whyItMatters: Air pollution is a recurring UPSC theme spanning environment, health, federal coordination and administrative accountability, and GRAP is the standard case study for emergency, graded environmental governance in India.

perspectives.take: Frames the story globally through the Swiss group's city ranking, positioning Delhi's pre-Diwali air as a headline international comparison rather than a domestic policy story.

static.topic: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Pollution: air pollution, environmental governance and institutions
static.whatIsIt: A set of emergency, pollution-level-linked measures for Delhi-NCR that are triggered in stages as the Air Quality Index worsens, ranging from dust control and mechanised sweeping to construction bans, vehicle restrictions and work-from-home advisories.
static.background: GRAP was formulated in 2016 by the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority on directions of the Supreme Court, which had asked for a graded emergency plan in the M.C. Mehta litigation, and was notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2017. Implementation passed to the Commission for Air Quality Management after the CAQM Act, 2021. The stages were re-specified in 2022 with clearer thresholds and a longer list of actions.
static.geography: Applies to Delhi and the contiguous NCR districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, a region marked by winter temperature inversion, low wind speeds and the Indo-Gangetic Plain's topography that traps pollutants.
static.socioEconomic: Curbs fall unevenly — construction workers, daily-wage labour, small traders and transport operators bear immediate income losses, while the health burden of PM2.5 falls most heavily on children, the elderly and outdoor workers.
static.whyInNews: Stage III restrictions continue in Delhi-NCR even as the AQI eased to the 'very poor' band, and enforcement notices have been issued to private establishments in Gurgaon.
static.wayForward: Link stage revocation to transparent, published air-quality data; compensate affected informal workers during curbs; shift from episodic emergency action to year-round source-specific abatement across the NCR airshed.
prelimsPointers: GRAP was prepared in 2016 on Supreme Court directions and notified by MoEFCC in 2017; it is now implemented by the CAQM.

Stage III actions include bans on non-essential construction and demolition, restrictions on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers in the NCR, and a work-from-home advisory for a share of private-office staff.
Stage IV, the strictest, is invoked at 'Severe Plus' levels and adds measures such as restrictions on truck entry and suspension of most construction activity.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether a graded emergency plan can deliver clean air without parallel structural action on transport, industry, waste and biomass burning.

static.topic: Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Statutory and regulatory bodies; Centre-State relations
static.whatIsIt: A statutory body created by an Act of Parliament to coordinate air-quality planning and enforcement across Delhi and the NCR states, replacing the executive-era EPCA.
static.background: Set up by the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021, after the Supreme Court repeatedly pressed for a single empowered authority. It has powers to issue directions, frame plans and take coercive action, and its jurisdiction covers Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in the notified NCR and adjoining areas.
static.geography: Delhi-NCR and adjoining areas across five states, an airshed where pollutants travel across state boundaries irrespective of administrative jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: Cross-state enforcement raises federal friction: farm-fire restrictions in Punjab and Haryana, industrial norms in UP and Rajasthan, and transport curbs in Delhi impose different costs on different constituencies.
static.whyInNews: GRAP stage decisions and enforcement action in the current pollution episode are being driven by the CAQM framework.
static.wayForward: Strengthen airshed-level planning, publish source-apportionment and enforcement data, and build state-level accountability mechanisms rather than relying on ad hoc directions.
prelimsPointers: CAQM is a statutory body under the CAQM Act, 2021, and replaced the EPCA, which was created through executive order in 1998.
Its jurisdiction extends to Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in the notified National Capital Region and adjoining areas.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how far a single statutory airshed regulator resolves the coordination problems of multi-state environmental governance.

static.topic: National Clean Air Programme and India's AQI framework
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Environmental pollution and degradation; conservation
static.whatIsIt: The National Clean Air Programme is the Centre's city-based framework for reducing particulate pollution, while the AQI is the CPCB's eight-pollutant index used to communicate air quality and trigger GRAP stages.
static.background: NCAP was launched in January 2019 with a target of 20–30% reduction in PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by 2024 over the 2017 base year; the target was revised in 2022 to a 40% reduction in particulate concentrations by 2025-26 for the covered cities. The AQI, launched in 2014, runs from 0 to 500 across six categories — Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor, Severe — with 'Severe Plus' used for the 451–500 band.
static.geography: NCAP covers over a hundred non-attainment cities identified by the CPCB on the basis of persistently poor air quality; the AQI is reported for major cities nationwide.
static.socioEconomic: Air pollution is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular morbidity, lost working days and reduced life expectancy, with the poorest households least able to shield themselves.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's AQI reading of 364 places it in the 'very poor' category and keeps the city at the top of global pollution rankings.
static.wayForward: Move from city-level targets to airshed-level plans, expand real-time monitoring networks, and integrate health and transport data into clean-air planning.
prelimsPointers: The AQI has six categories: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500).
NCAP was launched in January 2019 and its particulate-reduction target was revised in 2022 to 40% by 2025-26 over the 2017 base year.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the adequacy of India's clean-air policy architecture in converting emergency measures into durable reductions in particulate pollution.

prelims: Delhi's AQI was reported at 364, in the 'Very Poor' band (301–400), while Stage III GRAP curbs continued because revocation requires sustained improvement rather than a single day's reading.
GRAP stages are linked to AQI bands: Stage I at 'Poor', Stage II at 'Very Poor', Stage III at 'Severe' and Stage IV at 'Severe Plus'.
GRAP was framed in 2016 on Supreme Court directions and notified by MoEFCC in 2017; it is now implemented by the statutory CAQM under the CAQM Act, 2021.
The Gurgaon district administration issued notices to private law firms for alleged violation of pollution-related office norms, showing that GRAP obligations extend to commercial establishments.
stories.mainsQuestion: Delhi's annual air-quality emergency is met with a predictable cycle of graded restrictions and equally predictable relaxation. Critically examine why the Graded Response Action Plan has not translated into durable improvements in air quality, and suggest institutional and policy reforms for airshed-level pollution control in the National Capital Region.

stories.headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Eisenkot with forming government
stories.summary: Israel's president has tasked Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and a leading rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with forming a government after the recent Knesset election left neither the incumbent's bloc nor the opposing bloc with a majority. Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, must now assemble a coalition commanding at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats. He has declined to seek the support of Arab parties, whose backing would have given him a working majority, sharply narrowing his options. If he fails, the mandate could pass to another Knesset member or the house could be dissolved, sending Israelis back to the polls.
stories.whyItMatters: A textbook case of coalition formation under proportional representation, useful for comparative-politics questions, and a reminder that political flux in West Asia directly touches India's energy, diaspora and connectivity interests.

static.topic: Israel's Proportional Representation and Coalition Government Formation
static.syllabusNode: Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries
static.whatIsIt: Israel is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral Knesset of 120 members elected nationally through proportional representation. The government must command the confidence of the Knesset, and the President — a largely ceremonial head of state — consults parties and designates a Knesset member to attempt government formation.
static.background: Israel has no single codified constitution; a set of Basic Laws serves as its constitutional foundation. The President is elected by the Knesset for a single seven-year term. Because the electoral threshold is low and the party system fragmented, no single party has ever won an outright majority, and Israel has held several early elections in recent years after coalitions collapsed.
static.geography: West Asia/Levant, on the eastern Mediterranean coast; borders Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt.
static.socioEconomic: High-income OECD member with a technology-driven economy and globally significant defence, agriculture and water-technology sectors.
static.whyInNews: The President has tasked Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu rival, with forming a government after no bloc won a majority in the recent election.
static.wayForward: Eisenkot must assemble 61 seats without relying on Arab parties; if he fails, the mandate may pass to another member or the Knesset may dissolve, triggering fresh elections.
prelimsPointers: Israel's Knesset is unicameral with 120 members elected by proportional representation from a single national constituency.
The President of Israel is elected by the Knesset for a single seven-year term and holds a largely ceremonial role.
Israel has no single written constitution; it is governed through Basic Laws.
static.mainsAngle: Compare coalition formation under proportional representation with India's first-past-the-post system, and assess how electoral design shapes government stability and accountability.

static.topic: India–Israel Relations
static.syllabusNode: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India and Israel maintain a strategic partnership spanning defence procurement, counter-terrorism, agriculture, water management, cyber and innovation, alongside India's longstanding political support for the Palestinian cause.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but established full diplomatic relations only in 1992. Ties deepened through defence cooperation and were elevated to a strategic partnership during the first Indian Prime Ministerial visit to Israel in 2017. India continues to balance this relationship with its historical ties to Palestine and its wider Gulf interests.
static.socioEconomic: Defence trade, agricultural technology such as drip irrigation and desalination, and growing labour mobility and people-to-people links.
static.whyInNews: A political transition in Israel could affect the continuity and pace of bilateral engagements.
static.wayForward: India should sustain engagement across Israel's political spectrum while preserving its traditional balancing act with Palestine and its interests in the wider Gulf.

static.socioEconomic: India sources a substantial share of its crude oil from West Asia and hosts a large diaspora in the Gulf, making remittances and energy security core stakes.
static.whyInNews: Israel's coalition uncertainty adds to the broader political flux in the region.
static.wayForward: Diversify energy sources, secure sea lanes, pursue de-escalation diplomacy and advance connectivity projects without over-committing to any single political outcome.

stories.headline: Saudi-led strikes near Sanaa kill dozens; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi oil, Riyadh airport
stories.summary: Airstrikes attributed to the Saudi-led coalition hit a village near Yemen's capital Sanaa, with the Houthi-run health ministry reporting at least 33 killed and 39 wounded, while a Houthi official cited 22 dead — footage from the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV showed children among the casualties carried into a local hospital. The Houthis said they launched six retaliatory operations targeting Saudi oil sites, Saudi troops and Riyadh airport. Separately, Syria denied reports that it planned to send troops to Yemen, even as its military ties with Saudi Arabia deepen. The exchange marks a fresh escalation in the decade-old conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government.
stories.whyItMatters: Escalation around Yemen directly affects Red Sea shipping, energy markets and India's crude supplies and Gulf diaspora — a recurring theme linking GS-II international relations with GS-III energy and maritime security. It also tests the limits of UN-led conflict resolution and regional de-escalation diplomacy.

static.topic: Yemen Civil War and the Houthi Movement
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Conflicts and West Asia
static.whatIsIt: A decade-long civil war in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) and Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has been backed since 2015 by a Saudi-led military coalition.
static.background: The Houthis, a Zaidi Shia revivalist movement from the northern governorate of Saada, seized Sanaa in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 (Operation Decisive Storm), and UNSC Resolution 2216 (2015) demanded Houthi withdrawal from seized territory. The Stockholm Agreement (2018) addressed Hodeidah, and a UN-brokered truce that began in April 2022 lapsed in October 2022. A UN Special Envoy continues to mediate.
static.geography: Yemen sits at the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman, and commands the Bab-el-Mandeb strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
static.socioEconomic: The conflict has produced one of the world's worst humanitarian crises — mass displacement, food insecurity, cholera outbreaks and a collapsed economy — with aid access repeatedly disrupted.
static.whyInNews: Airstrikes attributed to the Saudi-led coalition near Sanaa killed dozens according to Houthi-run health authorities, and the Houthis claimed retaliatory operations against Saudi oil sites, troops and Riyadh airport.
static.wayForward: A durable UN-mediated political settlement, sustained de-escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition, and unimpeded humanitarian access.
prelimsPointers: UNSC Resolution 2216 (2015) demanded that the Houthis withdraw from territory they had seized and imposed an arms embargo.
The Bab-el-Mandeb strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a critical global shipping chokepoint.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how the Yemen conflict illustrates the limits of multilateral conflict resolution and the spillover of regional rivalries into global trade routes.

static.topic: India and West Asia: Energy, Diaspora and Diplomacy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Extended Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: India's West Asia policy balances energy imports, a large expatriate workforce and remittances, trade and investment, and maritime security cooperation with Gulf states, while staying outside regional military coalitions.
static.background: India launched the 'Look West' policy in 2005, deepened engagement with the Gulf Cooperation Council, and elevated ties with Saudi Arabia to a Strategic Partnership Council in 2019. The India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) was announced on the sidelines of the 2023 G20 New Delhi Summit.
static.geography: West Asia holds the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb–Red Sea route, through which a large share of India's crude oil and westbound trade passes.
static.socioEconomic: An estimated eight to nine million Indians work in the Gulf; their remittances form a large share of India's annual remittance inflows, and conflict there directly threatens livelihoods and triggers evacuation contingencies.
static.whyInNews: Renewed Saudi–Houthi escalation, including Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and Riyadh airport, raises immediate questions for India's energy supplies and diaspora safety.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing and strategic reserves, strengthen maritime escort and evacuation readiness, and continue quiet diplomacy with both Iran and Gulf partners.
prelimsPointers: India's Strategic Partnership Council with Saudi Arabia was set up in 2019 during the Prime Minister's visit to Riyadh.
IMEC was announced at the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi by India, the US, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the EU, France, Germany and Italy.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how instability in West Asia tests India's balancing act between energy security, diaspora protection and strategic autonomy.

static.topic: Maritime Security and Sea Lanes of Communication in the Indian Ocean Region
static.syllabusNode: Security — Maritime Security; Economy — Energy Security
static.whatIsIt: Protection of sea lanes of communication and chokepoints through which India's trade and energy imports flow, primarily the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab-el-Mandeb–Red Sea corridor and the Suez route.
static.background: The Indian Navy has run anti-piracy and escort missions in the Gulf of Aden under Operation Sankalp since 2019, and conducted Operation Raahat in 2015 to evacuate Indian and foreign nationals from Yemen. Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea from late 2023 prompted expanded Indian Navy deployments.
static.geography: The Red Sea–Bab-el-Mandeb–Gulf of Aden corridor links the Suez Canal to the Indian Ocean; disruption forces shipping around the Cape of Good Hope, raising freight and insurance costs.
static.socioEconomic: Longer routes raise India's import bill and export freight costs, feeding into inflation and current-account pressure.
static.whyInNews: Escalation around Yemen revives the risk of disruption along the Red Sea route that carries a substantial share of India's westbound trade.
static.wayForward: Sustained naval presence, information-sharing with regional partners, and diversification of routes and suppliers.
prelimsPointers: Operation Sankalp is the Indian Navy's maritime security operation in the Gulf of Aden and adjoining waters, begun in 2019.
Operation Raahat (2015) evacuated Indian nationals and foreign nationals from war-torn Yemen.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the strategic and economic consequences for India of chokepoint insecurity in the Red Sea corridor, and evaluate the adequacy of India's maritime response.

prelims: Casualty figures near Sanaa are contested: the Houthi-run health ministry (via the Saba news agency) reported 33 killed and 39 wounded, while a Houthi official cited 22 dead — figures relayed largely through Houthi-run media.
The Houthis said they carried out six operations targeting Saudi oil sites, Saudi troops and Riyadh airport; the group is Iran-backed and fights a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government.
Sanaa has been held by the Houthis since 2014, and the Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015.
Syria denied reports that it would send troops to Yemen, even as its military ties with Saudi Arabia deepen.
stories.mainsQuestion: West Asia's chronic instability repeatedly spills over into India's energy supplies, trade routes and diaspora interests. Examine the implications of the renewed Saudi–Houthi escalation for India and suggest a calibrated diplomatic and maritime-security response.

stories.headline: Ten years on, demonetisation judged a failure on its own goals
stories.summary: As the tenth anniversary of the 8 November 2016 withdrawal of Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes approaches, two retrospectives conclude the exercise did not deliver on its stated objectives of curbing black money, fake currency and terror financing. Scroll.in argues that cash has retained its dominance in the economy, and that while UPI transaction volumes have risen sharply, the average value per transaction remains low, limiting the claim of a decisive shift to digital payments. The Hindu's opinion piece shifts the lens to public health, documenting the hidden costs of the sudden cash shortage — disrupted out-of-pocket spending on care, and the burden on poor households and informal workers who transact entirely in cash. Together the pieces frame demonetisation less as a one-off shock and more as a lasting lesson in how liquidity, and not merely digital adoption, underwrites welfare and health access.
stories.whyItMatters: Demonetisation is a standing case study for UPSC on policy design, executive action versus legislative scrutiny, and the real-world limits of digital public infrastructure. It is routinely used to test evaluation of welfare delivery, the informal economy and the cash-versus-digital transition.

perspectives.take: A sharply critical retrospective calling the exercise a resounding failure on all its own objectives, noting that cash remains king and that high UPI volumes mask low transaction values; written from a progressive, policy-accountability standpoint.
Coverage available at source.

static.topic: Demonetisation and the UPI-led digital payments shift
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data: Digital Public Infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure is a layered, interoperable stack built on identity (Aadhaar), payments (UPI) and document storage (DigiLocker). UPI, run by NPCI, is the payments layer that demonetisation is credited with accelerating.
static.background: Aadhaar was rolled out by UIDAI from 2009 as the world's largest biometric ID system. UPI was launched by NPCI in 2016, the same year as demonetisation, and now processes billions of transactions a month. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 subsequently created a consent-based framework with a Data Protection Board to govern personal data processing.
static.geography: Pan-India in coverage; adoption of digital payments is concentrated in urban and semi-urban areas, while rural and elderly users remain comparatively cash-dependent.
static.socioEconomic: Digital payment growth has lowered transaction costs and aided formalisation, but small average ticket sizes and continued cash use among low-income and informal households limit the inclusion dividend.
static.whyInNews: Ten years after demonetisation, retrospectives assess whether it genuinely shifted India from cash to digital and note that high UPI volumes coexist with low transaction values.
static.wayForward: Treat digital payments as a complement to, not a replacement for, cash in the short run; expand rural connectivity, merchant acceptance and financial literacy, and use the DPDP Act framework to address privacy and fraud risks.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
UPI was launched in 2016, the same year as demonetisation.
The DPDP Act, 2023 provides for consent-based processing, data-principal rights and obligations for significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's DPI-led payments transition has advanced financial inclusion or created new exclusion for cash-reliant households; balance innovation with privacy and state surveillance concerns.

static.topic: Cash dependence, welfare delivery and the health costs of demonetisation
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Architecture, Rights & Delivery
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model combines rights-based laws (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009, NFSA 2013) with DBT-enabled schemes riding the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone. Cash-reliant groups remain vulnerable when liquidity is disrupted.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat (2018) carries a health insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health and Wellness Centres; POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. Article 15 and 16, read with Indra Sawhney (1992), frame reservation policy. DBT and the JAM trinity reshaped subsidy delivery in the 2010s.
static.socioEconomic: Households without banking buffers or digital access bore the sharpest costs of the 2016 cash crunch, including deferred health spending — pointing to exclusion errors in a delivery system that assumes formal finance.
static.whyInNews: The Hindu's opinion piece links demonetisation to hidden public health costs arising from cash shortages, reinforcing the case for preserving liquidity alongside digital welfare delivery.
static.wayForward: Retain cash and banking correspondent channels alongside DBT, build household-level liquidity buffers for health emergencies, and design welfare delivery that does not presume continuous digital or banking access.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
PM-JAY is the health-insurance arm of Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018.
static.mainsAngle: Welfare exclusion errors and the shift from entitlement to capability; assess whether digital-first delivery widens or narrows the gap for informal and cash-dependent households.

static.topic: Demonetisation by notification: executive action and parliamentary oversight
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). The 2016 demonetisation, by contrast, was effected through an executive notification rather than a fresh parliamentary statute.
static.background: The earlier demonetisation of high-denomination notes in 1978 was backed by the High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978, whereas the 2016 measure was issued under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, through a Gazette notification. Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can delay but not amend them on money provisions. Ordinances (Article 123) must be approved within six weeks of Parliament reassembling. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills.
static.socioEconomic: Major economic decisions taken by notification raise questions of accountability and predictability for households and small firms, especially where no legislative debate or committee scrutiny precedes them.
static.whyInNews: The tenth-anniversary retrospectives reopen the question of how a sweeping economic measure was imposed — through executive notification — and what that implies for legislative scrutiny.
static.wayForward: Strengthen ex-ante parliamentary and committee scrutiny of measures with economy-wide effects; codify threshold tests and consultation requirements for delegated economic powers.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
An ordinance must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of reassembly.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and committee referrals; use demonetisation to debate the limits of delegated economic powers and parliamentary productivity as a governance indicator.

prelims: On 8 November 2016, Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes — roughly 86% of currency in circulation by value — were withdrawn from legal tender.
RBI later reported that about 99.3% of the demonetised notes, by value, were returned to the banking system.
UPI was launched by NPCI in 2016; demonetisation is often credited with boosting its adoption, though average transaction values have stayed small.
The 2016 measure was issued by Gazette notification under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, unlike the 1978 demonetisation which rested on a dedicated Act of Parliament.
stories.mainsQuestion: Demonetisation was justified in 2016 on the grounds of curbing black money, counterfeit currency and terror funding, and of pushing India towards digital payments. Critically evaluate its outcomes a decade later, and discuss what the episode teaches about the design of India's cash-to-digital transition and the welfare costs of liquidity shocks. (250 words, 15 marks)

stories.headline: New Zealand election leaves no clear winner; coalition talks loom
stories.summary: New Zealand's general election on 7 November 2026 produced provisional results in which neither the governing National-led coalition nor the opposition Labour Party reached a majority, leaving the shape of the next government undecided. Reporting through 8 November pointed to a highly fragmented parliament in which minor parties — including a rising Opportunity Party — hold the balance, and in which National won more electorate seats than its party vote alone would have delivered. Te Pāti Māori's capture of five Māori seats contributed to a provisional parliamentary overhang of roughly nine or ten seats, further complicating the arithmetic of any majority. With no combination yet able to command confidence, incumbent Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's administration continues in a caretaker capacity while coalition negotiations proceed, a process that could take weeks.
stories.whyItMatters: A hung parliament in a Westminster-derived democracy is a live case study in coalition formation, caretaker conventions and the representativeness of different electoral systems — recurrent themes in UPSC questions on comparative constitutionalism, legislature and representation.

perspectives.take: Carries the Reuters wire's procedural framing — an explainer on what happens after the vote, plus a profile of 38-year-old first-term MP Qiulae Wong as a possible holder of the balance of power.

Academic, explanatory framing: the election was 'all about the maths', with the electorate-seat versus party-vote mismatch and the nine-or-ten-seat overhang central, plus a companion piece on how caretaker government operates.

static.topic: Hung Parliament, Coalition Formation and Caretaker Government (comparative)
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Parliament and Legislative Process; Comparative Constitutions
static.whatIsIt: In a parliamentary system the executive derives its mandate from a majority in the legislature. When no party or pre-election alliance reaches that majority, government formation depends on post-election coalition bargaining, and the incumbent administration stays on in a caretaker capacity until a new government is sworn in.
static.background: India's Constitution vests Parliament in the President and two Houses (Article 79), and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75). Conventions sharpened after the hung Lok Sabhas of 1989–1996 require the President to satisfy himself that a claimant can command a majority, often through a floor test. Westminster-derived systems such as New Zealand rely on written or conventional caretaker rules that confine an outgoing government to routine business pending the formation of a new one.
static.whyInNews: New Zealand's 7 November 2026 provisional results left no bloc with a majority, producing a caretaker government under incumbent Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and weeks of expected coalition talks.
static.wayForward: The relevant lesson for India is procedural robustness: codified caretaker conventions, time-bound floor tests and transparent coalition agreements reduce uncertainty during transitions.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
In a hung House the President invites the leader most likely to command a majority, typically requiring a floor test.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how caretaker conventions and floor tests safeguard constitutional continuity during hung parliaments, comparing India's practice with Westminster-derived systems.

static.topic: Electoral Systems: First-Past-the-Post versus Proportional Representation (MMP)
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Elections, Representation and Electoral Reform
static.whatIsIt: Electoral systems translate votes into seats. First-past-the-post (FPTP) elects the highest-polling candidate in each constituency; proportional systems allocate seats broadly in line with vote share; Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) combines single-member electorates with a party-vote list element.
static.background: New Zealand used FPTP until a 1993 referendum endorsed MMP, first applied in the 1996 election. Under MMP voters cast both an electorate vote and a party vote, seats normally total about 120, and an overhang arises when a party wins more electorate seats than its party-vote entitlement. India retains FPTP for the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, a design often criticised for large vote-to-seat distortions.
static.geography: New Zealand is a South Pacific island nation; India's FPTP operates across a far larger and more socially diverse electorate.
static.socioEconomic: Proportional systems tend to increase the number of effective parties and make coalitions the norm, which affects how regional and minority interests secure representation.
static.whyInNews: The 2026 New Zealand result — a provisional overhang of nine or ten seats and a fragmented parliament — illustrates how electoral-system design shapes government formation.
prelimsPointers: New Zealand adopted MMP through a 1993 referendum and used it first in the 1996 general election.
An overhang seat arises when a party's electorate-seat wins exceed its proportional entitlement.
India uses the FPTP, single-member constituency system for Lok Sabha elections.
static.mainsAngle: Does India's FPTP system adequately translate voter preferences into representation? Discuss with reference to debates over proportional representation and coalition stability.

prelims: New Zealand's 7 November 2026 general election returned provisional results with no bloc holding a majority; the incumbent National-led coalition continues as a caretaker government.
Reporting put the provisional parliamentary overhang at nine or ten seats, with Te Pāti Māori winning five Māori seats.
New Zealand has used the Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system since the 1996 election, following a 1993 referendum.
Coalition negotiations after an inconclusive New Zealand election can run for weeks before a new government is sworn in.
stories.mainsQuestion: Coalition governments formed after inconclusive elections test the conventions of parliamentary democracy. Compare the safeguards available in India with those in Westminster-derived systems such as New Zealand, and assess whether India needs a codified caretaker-government framework.

stories.headline: Explosions reported in southern Iran; US disables cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman
stories.summary: Explosions were reported in southern Iran and on Qeshm Island, with Iranian state television saying officials had not confirmed any missile strikes and the semi-official Tasnim agency citing a source that the Qeshm blasts were not missile-related. The reports came alongside a US Central Command statement that American forces disabled a St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after it tried to leave regional waters having visited an Iranian port; a US aircraft fired precision munitions at the ship's stern after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. Separately, US President Donald Trump was reported as describing a strike on an anti-aircraft device on Qeshm Island as "minor". Accounts remain contested, with no independent confirmation of the cause of the explosions, the legality of the interdiction, or any casualties.
stories.whyItMatters: Escalation in West Asia directly touches India's crude and LNG supplies, its Gulf diaspora and its connectivity projects, while the episode is a live case study on unilateral use of force, freedom of navigation and the limits of the UN Security Council.

perspectives.take: Wire-style and attribution-heavy: reports Iranian state TV's non-confirmation of missile strikes and Tasnim's denial of a missile link on Qeshm, while separately carrying CENTCOM's own account of disabling the vessel — no independent verification offered.
Headline-level aggregation of the same Iranian media reports with minimal detail; frames the explosions as unverified and avoids attributing responsibility.

static.topic: UN Security Council, Use of Force and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Multilateralism
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: A US military action against a cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and reported explosions in southern Iran revive questions about unilateral use of force and the Security Council's capacity to arbitrate US–Iran tensions.
static.wayForward: India should keep pressing for UNSC reform through the G4 and IGN while protecting its strategic autonomy; de-escalation in West Asia is best pursued through regional dialogue and multilateral channels rather than unilateral action.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent (with veto) plus 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ sits at The Hague; the UN headquarters is in New York.
India is a founding UN member and among the largest contributors to UN peacekeeping.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the UN Security Council's structure and veto politics leave it ineffective in containing unilateral military action in West Asia.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz, Qeshm Island and India's Energy Security
static.syllabusNode: Geography — World Geography: Strategic Straits and Chokepoints
static.whatIsIt: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow passage linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea; Qeshm Island, Iran's largest island, lies within it. Roughly a fifth of global oil trade transits the strait.
static.background: Hormuz has been a recurring flashpoint — tanker attacks and seizures in 2019, the US killing of Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani in 2020, and periodic Iranian threats to close the strait. India's Chabahar port project in Iran and the International North–South Transport Corridor add a connectivity dimension.
static.geography: The strait narrows to roughly 39 km at its narrowest, with shipping lanes running through Omani and Iranian waters under the transit-passage regime.
static.socioEconomic: India sources a large share of its crude oil and LNG from West Asia; disruption raises freight, insurance and crude prices, pressures the rupee and the current account, and affects the large Indian diaspora in the Gulf.
static.whyInNews: Explosions were reported on Qeshm Island and in southern Iranian cities, and the US disabled a cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after it had called at an Iranian port.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing and expand strategic petroleum reserves; deepen Chabahar and INSTC connectivity; maintain balanced ties with Iran, the Gulf states and the US.
prelimsPointers: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman; Qeshm is Iran's largest island.
Chabahar port lies in Iran's Sistan-Baluchestan province on the Gulf of Oman and is India's gateway to Afghanistan and Central Asia.
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserve facilities are at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
static.mainsAngle: Chokepoint disruptions in West Asia test India's energy security — evaluate India's diversification, reserve and connectivity responses.

static.topic: UNCLOS, Freedom of Navigation and Maritime Security
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law and Maritime Security
static.whatIsIt: UNCLOS (1982, in force 1994) is often called the constitution of the oceans: it sets the territorial sea (12 nm), contiguous zone (24 nm), exclusive economic zone (200 nm) and continental shelf, and guarantees freedom of navigation on the high seas and transit passage through straits used for international navigation.
static.background: India signed UNCLOS in 1982 and ratified it in 1995. The United States is not a party but treats most of UNCLOS as customary international law and conducts freedom-of-navigation operations.
static.geography: Straits used for international navigation — Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb and Malacca among them — are governed by the transit-passage regime under UNCLOS Part III.
static.whyInNews: The US disabling of a St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman raises questions about the legal basis for interdiction on the high seas and the scope of freedom of navigation.
static.wayForward: India should continue to uphold UNCLOS-based dispute settlement and freedom of navigation, and press for de-escalation through dialogue rather than unilateral interdiction.
prelimsPointers: UNCLOS was adopted in 1982 and entered into force in 1994; India ratified it in 1995.
Territorial sea: 12 nm; contiguous zone: 24 nm; EEZ: 200 nm.
The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) sits in Hamburg.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how unilateral maritime interdictions in the Gulf of Oman sit with UNCLOS and the principle of freedom of navigation.

prelims: US Central Command said a St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel was disabled in the Gulf of Oman after it tried to leave regional waters following a call at an Iranian port; a US aircraft fired precision munitions at its stern.
Iranian state TV said officials had not confirmed missile strikes on southern Iran, while the semi-official Tasnim agency cited a source saying the Qeshm Island explosions were not missile-related.
Qeshm Island, Iran's largest island, lies in the Strait of Hormuz; the strait links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
CENTCOM is the US unified combatant command responsible for the Middle East and Central Asia, headquartered at Tampa, Florida.
stories.mainsQuestion: Escalating US–Iran friction in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz poses a direct challenge to India's energy security and strategic autonomy. Examine the implications and outline a calibrated Indian response.

stories.headline: Jobs data: youth unemployment, poverty and the missing women managers
stories.summary: Three recent commentaries converge on India's jobs challenge: ORF argues the official youth unemployment rate undercounts labour-market distress by missing discouraged workers, unpaid family labour and informal work. Newslaundry's Hafta 614 turns to India's poverty numbers, situating them alongside the US midterm verdict and the politics of measurement. Mint reports a paradox in managerial pay: women earn more per hour than men in managerial roles, yet hold only 11.9% of such positions, with career progression and professional experience revealing persistent barriers. Together, the pieces suggest that headline employment and poverty indicators can obscure both youth underemployment and the pipeline problem that keeps women out of senior leadership.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, this links employment data quality, poverty measurement and gender inclusion to inclusive-growth debates in GS-III and social-justice questions in GS-II.

perspectives.take: Frames youth unemployment as a measurement problem: the headline rate misses discouraged, unpaid and informal workers, so policy may underestimate youth distress.

static.topic: Poverty, Inequality & Employment

static.whatIsIt: Poverty is measured by NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and by consumption surveys; employment by the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
static.background: NITI Aayog's National MPI (2021) uses 12 indicators across health, education and living standards. PLFS (since 2017) reports quarterly urban and annual all-India data. India became the world's most populous country in 2023.

static.topic: Welfare Architecture & Social Justice

The exercise also signals continued reliance on administered pricing, rather than pure market negotiation, as the primary tool for making critical medicines affordable.

static.topic: Drug Price Control in India — NPPA and DPCO
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Health Infrastructure, Pharmaceutical Sector and Pricing Regulation
static.whatIsIt: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), set up in 1997 under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, fixes and revises prices of medicines. It works through the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. Medicines listed in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) are 'scheduled' and subject to ceiling prices; non-scheduled formulations may see only a limited annual increase.
static.background: Price control of medicines in India dates back to the 1960s–70s, when a large share of formulations was under statutory control. Liberalisation from the 1990s progressively narrowed the controlled basket. DPCO 1995 shifted to a cost-based system, while DPCO 2013 moved to market-based pricing: the ceiling for a scheduled drug is computed from the simple average price of all brands with at least 1% market share, plus a retailer margin. The NLEM has been revised periodically, and in 2019 a set of anti-cancer medicines was brought under price control, followed by further revisions of the essential medicines list.
static.socioEconomic: Cancer care is among the most financially catastrophic categories of treatment in India, with long therapy cycles and high-cost drugs. Administered price cuts lower the entry cost of treatment, but affordability also depends on insurance coverage, generic substitution and the density of tertiary care facilities.
static.whyInNews: Revised prices of anti-cancer medicines became effective from Monday, with about 1,000 brands reduced and 203 left unchanged, yielding estimated annual savings of over ₹3,500 crore.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the evidence base for which drugs enter the essential list, rationalise trade margins across the supply chain, expand Jan Aushadhi generic availability, and pair price control with wider health-insurance coverage so that the benefit reaches patients who currently pay out of pocket.
prelimsPointers: NPPA was constituted in 1997 and functions under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.
DPCO is issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955; DPCO 2013 uses market-based pricing for scheduled drugs.
For scheduled medicines, the ceiling price is the simple average of prices of brands with at least 1% market share, plus a retailer margin.
Non-scheduled formulations are generally permitted an annual price increase capped at 10%.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether administered price ceilings on essential medicines are sufficient to improve affordability, or whether they must be complemented by insurance, generic promotion and supply-side reforms.

static.topic: Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme and the E20 rollout
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Infrastructure & Energy Security; Environment & Ecology — Biofuels
static.whatIsIt: A Central programme under which ethanol produced from sugar- and grain-based feedstocks is blended with petrol at increasing percentages, with E20 denoting a 20% ethanol blend. It is administered by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas through the Oil Marketing Companies, with fuel specifications laid down by the Bureau of Indian Standards.
static.background: The Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme began in 2003 on a pilot basis in selected states and was extended across the country in 2016. The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 widened permitted feedstocks, and its 2022 amendment advanced the blending timeline. The 20% blending target was moved up from 2030 to the mid-2020s, with the government reporting achievement of the average E20 blending milestone during the 2025 supply year. NITI Aayog's 'Roadmap for Ethanol Blending in India 2020-25' set out the scaling plan.
static.geography: Ethanol supply is concentrated in sugarcane- and grain-surplus belts — Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Bihar. Karnataka is among the larger producers of molasses-based ethanol, making it a significant node in the national blending supply chain.
static.socioEconomic: Blending links cane growers, sugar mills and standalone distilleries to the fuel market, supporting farmer realisations and mill cash flows while curbing the crude oil import bill and associated forex outflow. It simultaneously raises food-versus-fuel, water-use and land-use concerns, and shifts demand between sugar and grain feedstock depending on relative prices.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka's claim that ethanol-blended petrol samples failed quality norms, and the Centre's counter that the samples meet prescribed standards, have brought the certification and quality-assurance dimension of the E20 rollout into public focus.
static.wayForward: Transparent, jointly acceptable third-party testing protocols; clear and standardised labelling at retail outlets; wider consumer awareness on compatible vehicles and material-grade components; and periodic disclosure of blending data would help contain disputes and sustain public confidence in the programme.
prelimsPointers: The Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme was launched in 2003 and extended to the entire country in 2016.
BIS standard IS 17021:2018 specifies requirements for E20 fuel; ethanol itself is covered under separate BIS specifications.
Ethanol for blending is drawn from sugarcane juice, B-heavy and C-heavy molasses, sugar syrup, surplus and damaged food grains, maize and other feedstocks.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the push to E20 affects energy security, the sugar economy and consumer interests, and evaluate the institutional arrangements needed to assure fuel quality in a nationally mandated blending regime.

stories.headline: AI-led Wall Street selloff; Indian markets brace for volatility
stories.summary: A sharp selloff in AI-linked technology shares dragged US equities lower on November 5, 2026, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite all falling in a correction that analysts describe as unusually intense rather than routine. The trigger was mounting friction in the AI investment narrative that had powered much of the multi-year rally in US mega-cap technology stocks. Technical analysts expect the US benchmarks to find support and stage a relief bounce after some further weakness, while Indian commentary is more guarded: the Samvat 2083 rebound is seen as sustainable only if global risks ease and market breadth improves, with a near-term correction possible before the broader upmove resumes. In the US, a handful of mega-cap 'titans' have held up better than the wider market, and Berkshire Hathaway's decision to double its stock buyback has been read as a defensive signal. CNN framed the episode as a reminder of the age-old case for diversification rather than concentrated bets.

static.whatIsIt: The three headline US benchmarks — the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite — are the principal gauges of US equity performance and, by extension, of global risk appetite. The November 5, 2026 fall was concentrated in AI-linked technology names that had led the preceding rally, making it a valuation-and-narrative correction rather than a broad macro shock.

Since 2023, the AI investment theme — chips, data centres and hyperscalers — has driven a large share of US index gains, creating concentration risk that periodically unwinds sharply, as in the dot-com episode of 1999-2000.

static.socioEconomic: US index moves transmit to Indian households through mutual fund NAVs, ETFs, pension and insurance portfolios, and through the sentiment channel that shapes retail SIP behaviour. static.whyInNews: US equities crashed on November 5, 2026 on AI-theme friction, prompting Indian market commentary on whether the Samvat 2083 rebound can be sustained.
static.wayForward: For investors, diversification across sectors and geographies and valuation discipline; for policymakers, close monitoring of leverage, derivative exposures and cross-border flow volatility rather than reactive intervention.

static.whatIsIt: Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) is short-horizon, return-seeking capital invested in Indian equity and debt markets. Because it is liquid and sentiment-driven, it is the main channel through which a US selloff transmits to Indian indices, the rupee and the external accounts.
static.background: India opened its equity markets to foreign institutional investors in the early 1990s as part of liberalisation. The SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019 consolidated the earlier FII, FPI and sub-account categories into a single 'FPI' regime with three risk-based categories, and shifted registration to designated depository participants. FPIs are often described as 'hot money' because they can exit quickly during global risk-off episodes.
static.geography: India's deepening integration with global capital markets; sensitivity is highest in large-cap index constituents and in sectors with high foreign ownership.
static.socioEconomic: FPI outflows can weaken the rupee, widen the current account gap and raise domestic borrowing costs. Domestic institutional investors — mutual funds fed by monthly SIP flows, insurers and pension funds — have increasingly cushioned such shocks.
static.whyInNews: Indian markets are bracing for volatility after the November 5, 2026 US AI-led selloff, with commentary flagging global risks and weak market breadth.
static.wayForward: Deepen the domestic institutional investor base, maintain adequate forex reserves, keep external debt and current account deficits moderate, and avoid policy signals that amplify short-term flow volatility.
prelimsPointers: The SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 merged FIIs, FPIs and sub-accounts into a single FPI category with three risk-based groups.
FPIs are registered through designated depository participants.
FPI flows are classified as portfolio (not direct) investment and are inherently reversible.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the role of foreign portfolio investment in transmitting global financial shocks to India, and evaluate the adequacy of domestic institutional buffers such as SIP-driven mutual fund flows.

static.topic: Financial Stability and Asset-Price Concentration Risk
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Financial Stability; Banking and Markets
static.whatIsIt: Concentration risk arises when a small number of firms or a single investment theme accounts for a disproportionate share of index value and market activity. A sharp repricing of those names can impair collateral values, margin positions and leveraged exposures, turning a market correction into a financial stability concern.
static.background: The dot-com crash of 2000 and the global financial crisis of 2008 are the standard reference points for how concentrated asset-price booms unwind. In the post-2008 architecture, the United States created the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) under the Dodd-Frank Act, 2010, while the Reserve Bank of India publishes a Financial Stability Report twice a year assessing risks to the Indian financial system.
static.geography: Global — the AI trade is concentrated in US-listed firms but its financing and supply chains span Asia, including India's technology services and hardware import linkages.
static.socioEconomic: Household exposure to equity has risen through mutual funds, ETFs and pension products, so a sustained repricing affects consumption and wealth effects, not just institutional balance sheets.
static.whyInNews: The November 5, 2026 AI-led US selloff has revived questions about whether concentrated technology valuations pose a systemic risk.
static.wayForward: Strengthen macroprudential surveillance of leverage and margin funding, improve disclosure of concentration and liquidity risks in funds, and build cross-border coordination among regulators for globally interlinked asset markets.
prelimsPointers: The RBI publishes its Financial Stability Report twice a year, generally around June and December.
The Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) in the United States was created by the Dodd-Frank Act, 2010.
The dot-com crash of 2000 is the classic example of concentrated technology valuations unwinding.
static.mainsAngle: Do concentrated asset-price booms in a few technology firms constitute a systemic risk to the global financial system? Discuss with reference to the AI investment cycle and the tools available to regulators.

prelims: Dow Jones Industrial Average: 30 large US companies, price-weighted, dating to 1896; S&P 500: about 500 large-cap firms, float-adjusted market-cap weighted; Nasdaq Composite: launched 1971, technology-heavy.
The SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 consolidated FIIs, FPIs and sub-accounts into a single FPI category with three risk-based groups.
The RBI's Financial Stability Report is published twice a year; the US Financial Stability Oversight Council was set up by the Dodd-Frank Act, 2010.
Samvat is the Hindu calendar year followed by Indian markets; the new Samvat year traditionally opens with Muhurat trading on Diwali.
stories.mainsQuestion: Global equity markets have become increasingly sensitive to the AI investment cycle. Examine how such external shocks transmit to Indian capital markets, and suggest measures to strengthen domestic financial stability against global risk-off episodes.

stories.headline: Bombay High Court quashes Customs order that cited non-existent AI-generated judgments
stories.summary: The Bombay High Court has quashed a Customs Department order after it was found to rely on judgments that do not exist, apparently produced by an artificial-intelligence tool. The court treated the fabricated citations as a defect going to the root of the order's reasoning, holding that an administrative or quasi-judicial order resting on unverifiable authorities cannot survive judicial review. The episode points to the growing use of AI drafting tools in official and legal work without adequate human verification. It also raises wider questions about accuracy, accountability and due process in administrative adjudication as technology enters governance and court administration.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the integrity of judicial and quasi-judicial reasoning in an era of AI-assisted drafting, and links directly to Article 226 judicial review, administrative law and e-governance accountability — a recurring UPSC theme on technology, ethics and the rule of law.

perspectives.take: Legal-news framing: foregrounds the High Court's censure of an administrative order built on fabricated AI-generated citations, treating it as a caution on verification standards in legal and official drafting.
