static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: High Courts are constitutional courts established under Article 214, exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226; the Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and administrative action against the Constitution and the law.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 (SC) and 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court quashed a Customs order that relied on non-existent, apparently AI-generated judgments, underscoring the High Court's supervisory role over administrative and quasi-judicial adjudication.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise citation-verification protocols in administrative and judicial drafting, require disclosure of AI assistance, and build capacity through judicial academies; treat unverified AI output as a procedural defect capable of vitiating an order.
prelimsPointers: Article 214 provides a High Court for each state; Article 226 confers writ jurisdiction wider than Article 32.
Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) are constitutional remedies; Article 226 covers both fundamental and other legal rights.
Judicial review is treated as part of the basic structure and flows from Articles 13, 32, 226 and 227.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how courts should respond to AI-generated errors in pleadings and administrative orders, balancing efficiency gains against accuracy, due process and accountability.

static.topic: Artificial Intelligence in Governance and Justice Delivery
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance and use of technology in public administration
static.whatIsIt: Use of AI and machine-learning tools in government drafting, service delivery and court administration, including research assistants for judges and automated document generation.
static.background: NITI Aayog's National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2018) set out AI-for-all priorities spanning healthcare, agriculture, education, smart cities and mobility. The Supreme Court introduced SUPACE (Supreme Court Portal for Assistance in Court's Efficiency) in 2021 as a research-assistance tool for judges, explicitly not for deciding cases. India's stated approach treats AI as assisting, not replacing, human decision-making.
static.socioEconomic: AI adoption promises efficiency in drafting and case management but carries risks of error propagation, bias and opacity where outputs are not verified by a human decision-maker.
static.whyInNews: An administrative order quashed by the Bombay High Court had cited judgments that do not exist, illustrating the 'hallucination' risk when AI tools are used without verification.
static.wayForward: Adopt disclosure norms for AI-assisted drafting, human-in-the-loop verification, audit trails and training, aligned with data-protection and due-process safeguards.
prelimsPointers: NITI Aayog released the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in 2018.
SUPACE is the Supreme Court's AI-based research assistance portal for judges, introduced in 2021.
AI tools in Indian courts are assistive; judicial decision-making remains a human function.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the opportunities and risks of deploying AI in governance and justice delivery, and suggest safeguards to protect accuracy, accountability and due process.

prelims: The Bombay High Court quashed a Customs order that cited judgments which do not exist, reportedly generated by an AI tool.
Courts can set aside administrative or quasi-judicial orders that rest on non-existent or unverifiable legal authorities.
High Courts exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226, including certiorari to quash orders of tribunals and statutory authorities.
stories.mainsQuestion: The use of artificial intelligence in drafting official and legal documents raises questions of accuracy and accountability. In the light of recent judicial scrutiny of orders citing non-existent AI-generated judgments, discuss the safeguards needed to ensure due process in administrative adjudication. (250 words)

stories.headline: Kashmir militancy falls from 6,800 in 1996 to one, data show
stories.summary: Reported data indicate that the number of active militants in Jammu and Kashmir has fallen from roughly 6,800 in 1996 to a single individual at present. The trend is generally attributed to sustained counter-insurgency operations by the Army, CRPF and J&K Police, a denser intelligence and security grid, and a broad shift among local youth away from militancy. Development spending, employment schemes and rehabilitation of former militants are also cited as factors reducing fresh recruitment. At the same time, residual infiltration attempts and cross-border terror infrastructure mean the security challenge is not fully over, and the debate over the legal framework governing operations in the region continues.
stories.whyItMatters: A sharp, decades-long decline in active militancy is a core case study for GS-III internal security — it tests understanding of counter-insurgency strategy, the development-versus-security debate, and the AFSPA/disturbed-area framework in Jammu & Kashmir.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around official data showing a steep, decades-long fall in active militants, presenting it as evidence that Kashmir has turned away from militancy; a largely state-data-driven and optimistic framing.

articles.title: From 6,800 militants in 1996 to one now: How Kashmir has turned away from militancy
articles.snippet: From 6,800 militants in 1996 to one now: How Kashmir has turned away from militancy Deccan Herald

static.topic: Internal Security and Counter-Insurgency in Jammu & Kashmir
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security: terrorism, insurgency, role of external state and non-state actors
static.whatIsIt: Internal security covers terrorism, left-wing extremism (LWE), insurgency in the Northeast, and cyber/economic security, handled via the MHA, IB, NIA and state police. In Jammu & Kashmir it involves counter-insurgency operations, border management along the LoC, and deradicalisation.
static.background: Naxalism peaked in the 'Red Corridor'; the SAMADHAN doctrine guides counter-LWE. AFSPA applies to areas declared 'disturbed'. The Integrated Command and Control Centres and NATGRID support cyber security. In J&K, militancy peaked in the 1990s; AFSPA was extended to the state in 1990, and counter-insurgency has since been led by the Army, CRPF and J&K Police with an expanding intelligence grid.
static.geography: Jammu & Kashmir — the Kashmir Valley, Pir Panjal range and the Line of Control; Pakistan-occupied Kashmir lies across the LoC.
static.socioEconomic: Tourism, handicrafts and horticulture (especially apples) are highly sensitive to security disruptions; youth unemployment and alienation have historically fed recruitment, making livelihood generation central to counter-insurgency.
static.whyInNews: Reported data show active militants in Jammu & Kashmir declining from about 6,800 in 1996 to one at present.
static.wayForward: Consolidate gains through intelligence-led operations with human-rights safeguards, deradicalisation and rehabilitation programmes, police capacity building, and sustained employment and infrastructure investment in the Valley.
prelimsPointers: NIA (2008) investigates terror offences under the NIA Act.
CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response.
SAMADHAN doctrine guides India's counter-left-wing-extremism strategy.
static.mainsAngle: Development-versus-security approach; examine the cyber-threat landscape for critical infrastructure.

static.topic: AFSPA and the 'Disturbed Area' Framework
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security: role of armed forces, human rights concerns
static.whatIsIt: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act grants special powers to armed forces in areas declared 'disturbed' — powers of search, arrest and use of force, along with legal protection for actions done in good faith.
static.background: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958, was originally applied to Assam and Manipur and later extended to other parts of the Northeast; it was extended to Jammu & Kashmir in 1990. Areas are declared 'disturbed' by the Central Government or by the Governor/Administrator, and notifications are subject to periodic review and partial withdrawal.
static.geography: Applied in parts of the Northeast and Jammu & Kashmir; the footprint has been periodically reduced in some districts.
static.socioEconomic: Human-rights concerns and allegations of misuse have driven demands for repeal, while security forces argue the law is necessary where normal policing is not viable.
static.whyInNews: The reported near-elimination of active militancy has renewed debate on whether AFSPA's footprint in Jammu & Kashmir should be further reduced.
static.wayForward: Periodic review of disturbed-area notifications, phased withdrawal where policing capacity permits, stronger accountability mechanisms, and accelerated recruitment and training of J&K Police.
prelimsPointers: AFSPA was enacted in 1958 and extended to Jammu & Kashmir in 1990.
An area can be declared 'disturbed' by the Central Government or the Governor/Administrator of the state or union territory.
AFSPA has been partially withdrawn from some districts in the Northeast and J&K over time.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the decline in militancy justifies a phased withdrawal of AFSPA in Jammu & Kashmir.

prelims: Reported data place active militants in Jammu & Kashmir at about 6,800 in 1996 and one at present.
NIA (2008) investigates terror offences under the NIA Act.
CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response.
SAMADHAN doctrine guides India's counter-left-wing-extremism strategy.
stories.mainsQuestion: The reported near-elimination of active militancy in Jammu & Kashmir is often read as a vindication of a security-first approach. Critically examine this claim and suggest how a development-and-rights-based approach can consolidate the gains.

stories.headline: Kanpur tanneries still discharge untreated effluent into Ganga despite CETPs
stories.summary: An assessment reported by India Water Portal finds that untreated and partially treated effluent from Kanpur's leather tanneries continues to reach the Ganga even though common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) exist in the city. The gap is attributed less to the absence of infrastructure than to how consistently it is operated — capacity shortfalls, breakdowns, unreliable power and the recurring cost of running treatment units all push effluent past the plants. Weak monitoring, infrequent sampling and lax enforcement allow non-compliance to persist without consequence, so water quality gains do not hold. The account argues that durable improvement in the river depends on continuous regulatory enforcement and sustained industrial compliance rather than one-time plant construction.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a textbook case of the implementation gap in India's environmental governance — infrastructure exists on paper but enforcement and compliance determine actual river health. Useful for questions on pollution control, regulatory bodies and river rejuvenation.

perspectives.take: Frames the problem as one of consistent pollution control and enforcement rather than absence of treatment infrastructure — a water-sector specialist outlet, so it foregrounds compliance, monitoring and operational reliability over industrial economics.

articles.title: Kanpur’s tanneries and the Ganga: Why consistent pollution control matters
articles.snippet: Why does untreated effluent still reach the Ganga despite CETP facilities in Kanpur? Explore how regulatory enforcement and industrial compliance drive real water quality improvement.

static.topic: Namami Gange Programme and Ganga rejuvenation
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Conservation, Pollution and River Rejuvenation
static.whatIsIt: Namami Gange is the Union government's integrated mission for conservation and rejuvenation of the Ganga, implemented through the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) under the Ministry of Jal Shakti. It funds sewage and effluent interception, treatment infrastructure, riverfront development and biodiversity conservation.
static.background: The first structured effort was the Ganga Action Plan, launched in 1985, followed by GAP Phase II. The Ganga was declared India's National River in 2008, and the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) was constituted in 2009. NMCG was set up in 2011 as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and later given powers to issue directions under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Namami Gange was launched in 2014 as the umbrella mission consolidating these efforts.
static.geography: The Ganga basin is India's largest river basin, draining roughly a quarter of the country's geographical area and spanning multiple states including Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal. Kanpur, an industrial city in the middle Ganga plain, sits on the river's right bank.
static.socioEconomic: The river supports irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries and livelihoods for a very large population along its course, so pollution directly affects public health and rural incomes.
static.whyInNews: Continuing discharge of untreated tannery effluent in Kanpur shows that treatment assets alone have not translated into cleaner river water.
static.wayForward: Shift emphasis from asset creation to assured operation and maintenance, link funding to measured performance, strengthen real-time effluent monitoring, and enforce penalties for non-compliance.
prelimsPointers: NMCG is the nodal body for Namami Gange and functions under the Ministry of Jal Shakti; it is registered as a society (2011).
The Ganga was declared India's National River in 2008.
The Ganga basin is India's largest river basin, covering about a quarter of the country's geographical area.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate why river rejuvenation missions in India deliver infrastructure faster than they deliver water quality outcomes.

static.topic: Industrial effluent regulation and Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs)
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Environmental Pollution and Regulatory Institutions
static.whatIsIt: CETPs are shared treatment facilities set up for a cluster of small and medium industries that cannot individually afford full treatment. Regulation of industrial effluent rests on the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and directions issued by the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.
static.background: The Water Act, 1974 created the Central Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards, giving them powers to set standards and consent to operate. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 broadened the Centre's powers to issue directions, including closure and disconnection of utilities. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court dealt with tanneries discharging untreated effluent into the Ganga at Kanpur and directed remedial action. The polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle were affirmed by the Supreme Court in the mid-1990s.
static.geography: Kanpur's leather cluster is concentrated in the Jajmau area along the Ganga, making the river the immediate receiving water body for the cluster's effluent.
static.socioEconomic: Leather tanning is a major employer and export earner in Kanpur, but the sector is dominated by small units with thin margins, so the recurring cost of operating treatment plants competes directly with viability — a classic collective-action problem for CETPs.
static.whyInNews: Effluent continues to reach the Ganga from Kanpur tanneries despite CETP facilities, highlighting enforcement and operational failures.
static.wayForward: Ensure continuous power and dedicated funding for CETP operation, adopt real-time effluent monitoring linked to board dashboards, impose graded penalties and recovery of treatment costs from defaulting units, and strengthen State Pollution Control Board capacity for inspection.
prelimsPointers: CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974.
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the Centre to issue directions, including closure of polluting units.
A CETP serves a cluster of industries that cannot individually afford treatment infrastructure.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why common effluent treatment plants in India frequently underperform and suggest regulatory and financial reforms to ensure compliance.

static.topic: The Ganga river system and Himalayan rivers
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Drainage System and Physical Geography of India
static.whatIsIt: The Ganga is a snow- and glacier-fed Himalayan river, rising in the Gangotri glacier as the Bhagirathi and joining the Alaknanda at Devprayag to form the Ganga. It flows across the northern plains before draining into the Bay of Bengal, forming the Sundarbans delta with the Brahmaputra.
static.background: Himalayan rivers are perennial because they are fed by snowmelt and glaciers in addition to rainfall, unlike peninsular rivers which are largely rain-fed and seasonal. The Ganga's major tributaries include the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son and Damodar. The river's flow is strongly influenced by the monsoon, which delivers the bulk of annual rainfall between June and September.
static.geography: The Ganga plain is a vast alluvial tract supporting dense population and intensive agriculture. Kanpur lies in this plain on the right bank of the river in Uttar Pradesh, downstream of the Upper Ganga reaches and upstream of the confluence with the Yamuna at Prayagraj.
static.socioEconomic: The fertile alluvial plain and perennial water supply underpin agriculture, urban settlement and industry along the river, which is why pollution in the middle Ganga stretch has wide economic consequences.
static.whyInNews: Pollution from Kanpur's tanneries affects the water quality of the Ganga in its middle stretch, a perennial river with high dependence on its flows.
prelimsPointers: The Ganga rises as the Bhagirathi from the Gangotri glacier at Gaumukh and joins the Alaknanda at Devprayag.
Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow- and glacier-fed); peninsular rivers are largely seasonal.
Kanpur is located on the right bank of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the perennial character of Himalayan rivers interacts with industrial and urban pollution loads in the Ganga plain.

prelims: CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; State Pollution Control Boards operate under the same Act.
Namami Gange is implemented by the National Mission for Clean Ganga under the Ministry of Jal Shakti; the Ganga was declared the National River in 2008.
A CETP is a shared treatment facility for a cluster of industries; its effectiveness depends on continuous operation and maintenance, not merely on construction.
The Ganga basin is India's largest river basin, and Kanpur lies on the river's right bank in the middle Ganga plain.
stories.mainsQuestion: Industrial clusters such as Kanpur's tanneries continue to pollute the Ganga despite the presence of common effluent treatment plants. Examine the reasons for this implementation gap and suggest measures to make industrial effluent regulation in India more effective.

stories.headline: Fourth retired judge quits Bengal SIR appeal panels, process in doubt
stories.summary: A fourth retired judge appointed to hear appeals against deletions in West Bengal's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has resigned, further thinning the panel of 19 judges originally enlisted for the exercise. The resignations cast doubt on the Election Commission's ability to dispose of claims and objections within the SIR timetable, since these appellate panels are the designated forum for aggrieved electors. The ECI has defended SIR as a house-to-house verification exercise carried out under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, while opposition parties and civil-society groups argue that large-scale deletions combined with an understaffed appeal route risk disenfranchisement. With the appeal mechanism uncertain, the credibility of the final roll — and of the electoral events that follow it — is under scrutiny.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the Election Commission's institutional capacity and the fairness of electoral-roll revision, a recurring GS-II theme linking constitutional bodies, electoral reform and the right to vote.

perspectives.take: Kolkata-based national daily; frames the fourth resignation among the 19 retired judges as a fresh blow to the workability and credibility of Bengal's SIR appeal process, emphasising institutional strain over the merits of the revision itself.

static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections; Constitutional Bodies: Election Commission of India; Electoral Reforms
static.whatIsIt: A special, house-to-house verification exercise by which the ECI rebuilds an electoral roll afresh in a state or constituency, as distinct from the routine annual summary revision of rolls.
static.background: Electoral rolls are prepared by the ECI under Article 324 read with Sections 21–23 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. SIR was used on a large scale in Bihar in 2025 and subsequently extended to West Bengal, where the ECI appointed Designated Officers, Booth Level Officers and appellate panels of retired judges to hear claims and objections.
static.geography: West Bengal (state-wide roll revision); Bihar had an earlier comparable exercise.
static.socioEconomic: Roll errors and deletions affect welfare entitlements such as ration, PDS and MGNREGA that are linked to voter identity, and fall hardest on migrants, informal workers and the elderly who lack documentary proof.
static.whyInNews: The fourth of 19 retired judges appointed to Bengal's SIR appeal panels has resigned, raising doubts over the disposal of pending claims and objections.
static.wayForward: Publish panel composition and vacancy data, guarantee time-bound disposal of appeals with reasoned orders, apply transparent and verifiable criteria for deletions, and provide a clear statutory appeal route.
prelimsPointers: Electoral rolls are prepared by the ECI under Article 324 read with the RP Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
Form 6 is for inclusion of a new elector, Form 7 for objection to inclusion, and Form 8 for correction or transposition of entries.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether large-scale roll revision exercises can be reconciled with the constitutional guarantee of universal adult suffrage when the redressal machinery is understaffed.

static.topic: Election Commission of India — Independence and Quasi-Judicial Functions
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies; Appointment, Powers and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI, which also exercises quasi-judicial powers while deciding claims and objections relating to electoral rolls.
static.background: The ECI has been a multi-member body since 1993, comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners. In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023), the Supreme Court laid down a selection committee framework, later codified by the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The ECI has historically relied on retired judges and senior civil servants as observers and appellate authorities.
static.whyInNews: Resignations of retired judges from SIR appeal panels raise questions about the ECI's capacity to deliver credible, quasi-judicial redressal during a mass roll revision.
static.wayForward: Strengthen institutional capacity for redressal, publish reasoned appellate orders, and ensure appeal panels are adequately staffed and insulated from political pressure.
keyTerms: Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023
Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023)
prelimsPointers: The ECI became a multi-member body in 1993; the CEC can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a judge of the Supreme Court.
The 2023 Act provides for a selection committee consisting of the Prime Minister, a Union Minister nominated by the PM, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the credibility of the ECI depends not only on the conduct of polls but also on the transparency and robustness of its electoral-roll and redressal functions.

prelims: SIR is a special house-to-house revision of electoral rolls, distinct from the annual summary revision conducted by the ECI.
Claims and objections during roll revision are filed in Form 6 (inclusion), Form 7 (objection) and Form 8 (correction), with appeals to designated appellate authorities.
The ECI has used retired judges as appellate authorities in SIR-affected states; in West Bengal, 19 such judges were appointed, of whom four have now resigned.
stories.mainsQuestion: The credibility of an electoral roll revision depends as much on its redressal mechanism as on the revision itself. Examine this in the light of recent SIR exercises and the resignation of appellate judges.

stories.headline: US visa curbs push Indian IT firms to shift more work offshore
stories.summary: Fresh curbs on US work visas have revived the question of whether Indian IT services firms will move a larger share of technology delivery back to India. With onsite deployment in the United States becoming costlier and less predictable, companies are rebalancing their onsite-offshore mix, expanding India-based delivery capacity and hiring more locally in the US. Analysts caution that any shift will be gradual, because client-facing roles, data-security obligations and contractual commitments still require a physical US presence. The episode underlines the sector's structural exposure to US immigration policy at a time when North America remains its single largest revenue market.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the resilience of India's largest services export earner and its external sector against a developed-country policy shock, directly linking migration policy to India's growth, employment and current-account story.

perspectives.take: Frames the visa curbs as a live strategic question for Indian IT — whether costlier US mobility will finally force a decisive shift of technology work offshore rather than a marginal rebalancing; a business-paper, industry-cost framing.

Argues that a change of political colour in Washington — a 'blue wave' — would not by itself relieve Indian IT, since visa restrictionism has become bipartisan; a technology-industry trade publication's sceptical, practitioner-facing framing.

static.topic: H-1B visa regime and Indian IT services
static.syllabusNode: Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests; Indian diaspora
static.whatIsIt: The H-1B is a US non-immigrant work visa for 'specialty occupations' requiring at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent. It is numerically capped, employer-sponsored and tied to a specific job, and Indian nationals have historically been its largest beneficiary group, with Indian IT services firms among its largest corporate users.
static.background: Created by the US Immigration Act of 1990, which set the base cap at 65,000 with a separate 20,000 set-aside for holders of advanced US degrees. The American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act, 2000, introduced 'H-1B dependent employer' attestation duties. A 2015 US appropriations law raised H-1B and L-1 fees for firms with 50-plus employees and a high share of such visa holders. Restrictions tightened during 2017-2021 through buy-American hiring guidance, higher denial rates and pandemic-era proclamations. In 2025 a US proclamation imposed a US$100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions, with carve-outs for existing visa holders and renewals; the measure has been contested in US courts.
static.geography: The US-India mobility corridor, with Indian delivery concentrated in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Noida-Gurugram and Mumbai.
static.socioEconomic: Affects the career paths of Indian engineers and their families, remittance flows, and the social-security contributions Indian professionals make in the US without reciprocal benefits — the basis of India's long-standing demand for a totalisation agreement.
static.whyInNews: Tighter US visa rules are raising the cost and uncertainty of onsite deployment, prompting Indian IT firms to reconsider how much work they deliver from the US.
static.wayForward: Diversify delivery through local US hiring, nearshore centres and India-based GCCs; deepen markets in Europe, Japan and the Middle East; pursue a bilateral totalisation and mobility framework; and move up the value chain so that revenue depends less on headcount deployed onsite.
prelimsPointers: H-1B base cap: 65,000 visas per year, plus 20,000 for holders of advanced degrees from US institutions.
India has consistently been the largest source country for H-1B beneficiaries.
A 2015 US law raised H-1B and L-1 fees for firms with over 50 employees and a high proportion of such visa holders.
L-1 visas cover intra-company transfers of managers and specialised knowledge workers, and are not subject to the H-1B numerical cap.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how immigration policy in developed economies acts as a non-tariff barrier to India's services exports, and evaluate the policy options available to India.

static.topic: Indian IT-BPM industry and services exports
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — services sector, growth, employment and changes in industrial policy
static.whatIsIt: India's IT and business process management (IT-BPM) sector spans software services, engineering R&D, business process outsourcing and digital transformation work. It is among the country's largest services export earners, a major source of foreign exchange, and one of the biggest employers in the organised private sector.
static.background: Growth began in the 1990s with the liberalisation of the Indian economy, the Y2K transition and the offshore delivery model built on cost arbitrage and English-speaking engineering talent. The 2000s saw scale-up through the onsite-offshore model; the 2010s brought automation, cloud and digital services; the 2020s have seen pressure from visa costs, wage inflation in the US, and the rise of in-house MNC captives.
static.geography: Tier-1 clusters in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Noida-Gurugram and Mumbai, with growing tier-2 presence in Coimbatore, Indore, Bhubaneswar, Kochi and Ahmedabad.
static.socioEconomic: Drives formal employment, urbanisation, engineering education demand and a large services trade surplus; North America accounts for the single largest share of its export revenue, creating concentration risk.
static.whyInNews: Visa curbs are forcing a reassessment of the onsite-heavy delivery model that has underpinned the sector's US revenue.
static.wayForward: Reduce dependence on headcount-linked onsite work; invest in AI, cloud, cybersecurity and product engineering; expand into Europe, Japan and the Gulf; and strengthen domestic digital public infrastructure and skilling pipelines.
prelimsPointers: IT and business services are among India's largest services export categories, with North America the largest single market.
The sector is a leading contributor to India's services trade surplus and to formal white-collar employment.
NASSCOM is the principal industry body representing the Indian IT-BPM sector.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how external policy shocks in destination markets affect India's services export model, and suggest measures to make the sector more resilient.

static.topic: Global Capability Centres and the future of offshore delivery
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — investment models, services sector, employment
static.whatIsIt: Global Capability Centres (GCCs) are in-house offshore units set up by multinational firms in India to deliver technology, engineering, analytics, finance and business-process functions. They differ from third-party IT outsourcing because the work is performed by the client's own employees.
static.background: They began in the 1990s as low-cost back offices and shared-service centres, then evolved into high-value hubs for R&D, product engineering, data analytics and AI. Their growth accelerated as MNCs sought talent at scale, and more recently as visa costs and geopolitical uncertainty made India-based delivery more attractive.
static.geography: Concentrated in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, NCR and Mumbai, with expanding presence in tier-2 cities.
static.socioEconomic: Creates high-value formal employment, fosters startup and deep-tech spillovers, and shifts value capture from third-party vendors towards MNC captives — changing the structure of India's IT labour market.
static.whyInNews: Visa curbs strengthen the business case for India-based delivery, benefiting both Indian IT services firms and MNC captives.
static.wayForward: Move GCCs up the value chain into product engineering and AI; strengthen talent pipelines and IP protection; and address data-localisation and cross-border data-flow concerns.
prelimsPointers: GCCs are in-house units of multinational companies, not third-party outsourcing vendors.
India hosts one of the world's largest concentrations of GCCs.
GCC growth is tracked by industry bodies such as NASSCOM and ANSR.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how the rise of GCCs is reshaping India's IT services landscape and what it implies for employment and value addition.

prelims: H-1B is a US employer-sponsored non-immigrant work visa for specialty occupations, capped at 65,000 plus 20,000 for advanced US degree holders.
India is the largest source country for H-1B beneficiaries, and Indian IT firms are among the largest corporate users.
A 2025 US proclamation imposed a US$100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions, with exemptions for existing visa holders and renewals; it has faced legal challenge.
L-1 visas, used for intra-company transfers, are not subject to the H-1B numerical cap.
stories.mainsQuestion: Tightening work-visa regimes in developed economies compel a structural rebalancing of India's IT services delivery model. Examine the implications for India's services exports, employment and external sector, and suggest policy responses.

stories.headline: Krakow old town shooting: six killed, far-right motive suspected
stories.summary: A gunman opened fire on random passers-by in the Main Square of Krakow's historic Old Town on Saturday, killing several people and injuring more than a dozen, according to Polish police. Initial reports put the death toll at five, while later police statements cited six dead; three further bodies were subsequently found at the attacker's home. Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the perpetrator is likely a domestic far-right extremist, pointing to a possible ideological motive rather than an organised plot. Investigations are continuing into the sequence of the attack and the suspect's background.
stories.whyItMatters: Feeds GS-III internal security questions on lone-actor and far-right terrorism, and GS-II discussions on European security cooperation and multilateral responses to transnational threats.

perspectives.take: Leads with the police account of a drive-by shooting at random people in the Main Square, putting the toll at five dead and twelve injured and treating motive as unconfirmed.
Wire-style casualty-focused report with no motive attribution, reflecting an early, fact-light framing of the incident.
Foregrounds the political dimension — Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski's assessment that the gunman is likely a domestic far-right extremist — and revises the toll to six.
Explanatory 'what we know so far' format that stitches the main-square killings to three bodies later found at the suspect's home, while stressing what remains unverified.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and UN Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN, founded in 1945, has six principal organs; the Security Council carries primary responsibility for international peace and security with five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for expansion of the Council. The Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: A mass-casualty attack in Poland, an EU, NATO and UN member state, renews focus on how national capitals and multilateral bodies coordinate against transnational security threats.
static.wayForward: Revive text-based negotiations in the IGN, build cross-regional coalitions, and address the Africa group's Ezulwini Consensus demand for representation.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; UN Headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent membership rests on representativeness, population and contributions; assess the obstacles posed by veto politics and competing regional claims.

static.topic: Far-right extremism and lone-actor attacks in Europe
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Extremism and Terrorism
static.whatIsIt: Far-right extremism covers nationalist, xenophobic, anti-immigrant and neo-fascist ideologies. Lone-actor attacks are carried out by individuals acting without formal organisational command, making them harder to detect through conventional intelligence channels.
static.background: Europe has seen a resurgence of far-right political parties and, alongside it, high-profile attacks linked to far-right or white-supremacist motives, including in Norway (2011) and Germany (Halle 2019, Hanau 2020). Online radicalisation and encrypted platforms have become key vectors.
static.geography: Poland is a Central European state, an EU and NATO member and part of the Schengen area; Krakow is its second-largest city.
static.socioEconomic: Immigration debates, economic anxiety and digital echo chambers are commonly cited drivers of far-right radicalisation across European societies.
static.whyInNews: Polish authorities suspect the Krakow gunman is a domestic far-right extremist, reviving debate on lone-actor terrorism in Europe.
static.wayForward: Strengthen intelligence-sharing through Europol, regulate extremist online content, and invest in deradicalisation and community-level prevention programmes.
prelimsPointers: Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, on the Vistula river; Warsaw is the capital.
Poland is a member of the EU, NATO and the Schengen area.
static.mainsAngle: Lone-actor attacks complicate traditional counter-terror frameworks; examine why and suggest reforms to European and global counter-terror cooperation.

static.topic: EU Firearms Directive and civilian gun control
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Arms Regulation and Comparative Gun Control
static.whatIsIt: The EU Firearms Directive (91/477/EEC) harmonises minimum rules on the acquisition and possession of civilian firearms across member states, categorising weapons and requiring licensing and record-keeping.
static.background: Adopted in 1991 and amended subsequently, the Directive was tightened in 2017 (Directive (EU) 2017/853) after a series of terrorist attacks, with stricter rules on semi-automatic firearms, deactivation and traceability.
static.geography: Applicable across EU member states, including Poland.
static.whyInNews: The Krakow shooting has revived European debate on civilian access to firearms and the enforcement of existing licensing rules.
static.wayForward: Improve enforcement and tracing, tighten deactivation standards, and use the Schengen Information System for cross-border alerts on prohibited persons.
prelimsPointers: The EU Firearms Directive 91/477/EEC was substantially amended in 2017.
The Directive is binding on EU member states, including Poland.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the EU's harmonised licensing approach with India's Arms Act framework and assess which elements are transferable to Indian conditions.

prelims: Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, located on the Vistula river in the country's south; Warsaw is the capital.
Poland is a member of the European Union, NATO and the Schengen area.
Poland's Interior Minister, as reported, is Marcin Kierwinski.

stories.mainsQuestion: Lone-actor attacks driven by far-right ideology are increasingly testing European internal security. Examine the causes of this trend and evaluate the adequacy of national and EU-level counter-measures, drawing lessons for India's own internal security architecture.
